reading.body:
Cyber cover for AI is being rewritten around losses that did not exist when the policies were drafted, and three of the ten exposures named here are physical rather than digital.

The ten items split into recognisable groups. Four are attacks on the model or its training data: indirect prompt injection through retrieved content, model inversion and extraction, poisoning, and synthetic media defeating biometric authentication. Two are supply chain: compromised packages in public model hubs, and zero days in widely deployed open source inference and orchestration frameworks. One is employee behaviour, staff uploading confidential material to unsanctioned tools. The remaining three sit at the physical and compute layer: ransomware on building control systems at data centres, stolen credentials used to run unauthorised GPU workloads, and war exclusions applied to state-sponsored attacks on compute infrastructure.

That last group is where this stops being a software story. Insurance language is a gate on deployment, because an operator cannot buy cover for a loss it has no name for. Naming building-control ransomware and compute hijacking as distinct exposures means the physical layer of AI is being priced as its own category, separate from the model that runs on it. War exclusions matter in the same place, since a state-sponsored attack on compute infrastructure is precisely the event the exclusion is written to remove from cover.

What this does not carry is any quantification. There are no loss amounts, premiums, claim counts, jurisdictions, or policy wording dates. It does not say which of the ten are already covered, which are excluded, and which are only proposed. It is a map of where the language is being contested, not a record of how it has been settled.
